analysis.one_liner: Automatically registers eligible voters when they turn 18 or interact with the DMV, with an opt-out.
analysis.headline: The automatic voter registration bill, sponsored by 9 Democrats with no Republican support, sat in the Senate Rules Committee without a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made voter registration the government's job rather than the voter's: every state would have to automatically register eligible citizens when they turn 18 and when they get or update a driver's license, unless the person opts out. It would have added privacy and security rules for registration data and sent states federal grants — $3 billion authorized for 2023 — to build the systems. It never advanced past its committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: Eligible citizens who are not registered or whose registrations are out of date — the bill's own findings single out young people, people with disabilities, and racial and ethnic minorities as those most hurt by today's paper-based, error-prone registration systems [S3]. Registered voters who move would have their addresses updated automatically through DMV records [S3]. States would receive federal grants to pay for the new technology [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Shifts the burden of registration from the voter to the government: states must automatically register every eligible citizen on their 18th birthday, and anyone who skips an election after moving would not lose their registration because the DMV would update it electronically.

Keeps registration voluntary — every person must be told they can decline, and declining cannot affect any state service, and a person's decision not to register may not be used against them in any proceeding.

Protects people from being prosecuted or having immigration problems because of a registration error they did not cause, while still allowing prosecution for anyone who knowingly files false registrations or votes illegally.

Adds safeguards: federal privacy and security standards for registration databases, public disclosure of all changes to voter rolls, a ban on commercial use of registration data, and annual state certifications — with grant money cut off for states that fail to certify.

Authorizes $3 billion for fiscal year 2023 in Election Assistance Commission grants so states — including states that already have automatic registration — can pay for electronic data transfer, online registration, and public education.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grant program ($3 billion authorized for FY2023, plus 'such sums as may be necessary' each year after). State motor vehicle agencies and election offices would take on the work of electronic data transfer, notices, and security compliance, with grants covering part of the cost; states that need to change their laws would have up to two years to comply, or until 2026 if they certify that meeting the 2024 deadline is impracticable [S3].

drawbacks.text: The cost is open-ended: the bill authorizes $3 billion for the first year alone and unlimited 'such sums as may be necessary' in later years, and states would still bear implementation work beyond the grants.

Automatic registration adds people to the rolls who did not ask to be registered, which can create inaccurate or duplicate records; the bill manages this with an opt-out, federal data-matching standards, and public logging of list changes rather than preventing it outright.

It is a federal mandate on how states run their own elections, pre-empting state registration procedures and requiring state election officials to certify compliance with national standards on pain of losing grant money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing a paperwork barrier that keeps eligible citizens off the rolls, with the heaviest impact on young, disabled, and minority voters — is large and permanent, and the bill's opt-out, privacy, and security provisions answer the most serious good-faith objections about accuracy and data protection. The main honest cost is money: a multibillion-dollar, open-ended federal grant program and real compliance work for state DMVs and election offices. The design is credible; the failure here was not the bill's content but that it was never seriously processed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2022 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 26, 2022, joined by eight other Democratic senators as original cosponsors; the cosponsor list later grew to 9 Democrats, with no Republicans.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration — the standard first step that hands a bill to the committee overseeing elections.
That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and incumbents kept the registration status quo — no federal mandate, no new spending, and no change to who is on the voter rolls. Voters who face registration barriers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State governments and the registration status quo

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MN); bill sponsor and Chair of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, the committee the bill was referred to
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded the referral to her own committee, which took no further action on it

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Blumenthal, Wyden, Leahy, Casey, Smith, Warren, Hirono, Booker, and one other)

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after receiving the referral

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which he controls the calendar for

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsor and no support for the bill

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 10 of the Senate's 50 Democratic caucus members — and not a single Republican signed on, so the bill had no path without Democratic leadership prioritizing it, which never happened.

industries.note: The bill would have created a multibillion-dollar grant stream for exactly what these firms sell: electronic data transfer between DMVs and election offices, online registration systems, and secure statewide databases. It explicitly allows agencies to hire third-party contractors to handle the data transmissions. The grants never materialized, so the industry got nothing.

The bill bans commercial use of registration data collected under it and shields declinations and personal details from disclosure, cutting off one commercial use of voter files. It leaves political and campaign use of voter data untouched.
